card: Call your credit card company and ask for a lower rate.
Right now, the average new credit card offer charges about 22.5%.
Say you owe $6,000 and pay $200 a month. It takes about 45 months to pay off, almost 4 years, and you hand the bank roughly $2,900 in interest.
Nearly half of what you borrowed, gone, just in interest.
Just ask. If you have a decent payment history, many people get their rate cut, sometimes by several points, from a single five-minute phone call. Most people never try.
mortgage: That's $255 more every single month. Over 30 years, that's more than $90,000, for the exact same house.
Right now, the average 30-year fixed rate is about 7.18%, according to Freddie Mac's weekly survey. That's actually down three weeks in a row. A year ago, it was around 6.22%.
On a $400,000 loan, a 6.22% rate is about $2,455 a month for principal and interest. At 7.18%, it's about $2,710.

If you already have a fixed-rate mortgage, a Fed hike doesn't change your payment at all. You're locked. If you have an adjustable-rate mortgage or a home equity line of credit, pay attention, because those usually do move with the Fed.
savings: At the average rate, you earn about $57 a year. In a top high-yield account, you'd earn about $435.
That's almost eight times more, for doing nothing except moving your money.
But here's the catch: most Americans keep their savings in the wrong place.

The national average savings account pays about 0.57%, according to Bankrate. That's barely more than nothing. But the top high-yield savings accounts pay around 4 to 4.35%. Same safety, same FDIC insurance, up to the legal limit. Completely different result.
If your savings account pays less than 1%, open a high-yield savings account. It takes about ten minutes, and it could earn you hundreds of dollars more a year.
